sentences.text: This meeting is being recorded.
Hi Nathan, how you doing?
Hi Andy, how are you?
Yeah, not too bad, thank you.
Not too bad.
Ah, there we go.
Hello.
How you doing?
We're good.
Pretty running around so you might hear some background sound.
Hopefully it's not too loud.
It's because we're in a hotel meeting room.
No, I can't hear it in the background.
All good, but you get my little dog there bark as soon as the door goes, so, so I, I apologize in advance.
Anyway, nice to meet you both.
I'm sorry about the mix up on the Times.
Not sure what happened there, but we've, we're all here now, so.
Yeah, be good to hear a little bit about what it is that you're looking for, Nathan, because I'm not 100 sure we can help.
So maybe before about us first.

So we're an M Advisory Capital A and we work with marketing agencies on the buy and the sell side, helping them to, to you know, either sell their business through agencies co, which is our marketplace, or buy businesses for our clients who are usually high growth agencies themselves or sometimes their investors or private equity or those types of firms that we help sort of target and build their businesses, portfolios, etc.
So yeah, it's normally marketing services.
I can see that you're offering some kind of ip, so be interested to kind of get an understanding of what it is and whether we can help.
Okay, maybe before we jump into it, just a couple more questions.
Your capital A, is it, Is it a US company or a UK company?
It's a UK company, but probably 95% of our work's US based, so.
And you're based in the US then?
No, I'm in the UK.
Okay.
Okay.
Okay.
Yeah, some of our team are US based as well.
New York and Los Angeles.
San Francisco.
Okay, and so you've worked in the marketing industry for quite a long time.
So I worked in marketing and media.
Yeah.
In 2016 I sold my business.
So after that I kind of got dragged into M and A buy.
But yes, I'm the CEO of capital A and all we do is M and A pretty much so.
Okay, great.
Well I think with your marketing background you'll probably be relatively receptive to what we've managed to develop.
So yeah, yeah, hopefully.
Okay, give it to me.
What is it Jonah?
Give the.
Yeah, the pitch.
World domination.
Brilliant.
No.
So both Nathan and I have worked half career in corporate marketing.
Nathan on the corporate side, I on the agency side.
And it's a mutual observation that led us to Start the development of the IP which we now want to put on the market.
The IP addresses something extremely fundamental in marketing and even by extent in commerce.
You're familiar with the sector.
I think we can agree that all that money is being spent has one finality, and that finality is to influence consumers, more precisely to influence what people value, like and buy.
Now, value attribution, emotional resonance.
Purchase decisions are the outcome of brain processes, mainly subconscious brain processes.
So go back to the beginning.
All that money in our industry is being invested with the finality to influence the brain processes that shape or govern what people value, like and buy.
Each type of marketing project, each type of marketing initiative has that same finality.
Now, the big elephant in the room is that that whole industry seeks to influence those processes without understanding those processes.
And it's blunt and bold claim, but it is very much the reality of the business.

I mean, we've come across hundreds of marketing managers, both on the agency side, on the brand side, on local levels, European levels, global levels, small organizations and the biggest brands in the world.
And none of those people actually know how the processes that they seek to influence work.
Now, you can compare that with, for instance, going to a doctor to treat your diabetes, but the doctor doesn't know the metabolic processes that control blood sugar.
It's really the state of the industry and it doesn't have to be like that.
Science in recent decades has made giant leaps and we come much closer to understanding how it all actually works in the brain.
But that science is not being used by the industry yet, despite how the industry portrays itself.
If you hear industry professionals speak, they will often pretend that they're really keeping the pace of all the scientific developments that makes them better at influencing people.
And so in reality, it's not the case at all.
It's not the case at all.
We've done now more or less 50 important projects for the biggest brands on the world on a global level, using our innovation.
And we always observe that it's not the case at all.
I think this is simply.
I was seeing you frowning a bit, Andy, but I don't know what topic it was that we were saying that there was more frowning or less frowning.
But if you've been in the industry for quite a while, you've probably met a huge amount of people working in the industry.

If you were to ask them the simple question of which brain processes control what people value or which process to control what people like and buy, most of them wouldn't be able to give you an answer.
No.
So there's already there a huge knowledge gap, let alone talking about the frameworks, the business procedures, the research technology that they use to try and understand this.
There's even bigger gap on those topics.
So there's a knowledge gap and there's a gap in the whole marketing toolkit which is in disconnect with those brain processes which control consumer behavior.
Specifically on those three topics, what people value, what people like and what people buy.
Those are the three topics we, we are experts within.

And so what we've done over the last decade is we've worked with senior scientists from leading universities to develop an overarching framework, clear understanding of those brain processes, and to develop business solutions which solve both strategic marketing challenges such as recruitment, value for money, loyalty, brand positioning, all these things.

And also a whole range of operational marketing initiatives such as campaign development, packaging development, all the type of product development, product development, sponsoring platforms, which kind of brand ambassador do you need to choose?
And we develop those in accordance with those brain processes and then we've validated it across 30 or 40 countries working with the global entities of world class brands.
When we talk about global entities of world class brands, we're talking about companies such as Chanel.
On a global level, we're talking about Companies such as L'Oreal, Unilever, PepsiCo, PepsiCo, Richemont, IKEA, IKEA, Novartis, we've worked with them.
Why and how?
We're, as I said, we don't have an agency, we're a two man show, we don't have a name within the agency industry.
And these big brands are working with the best agencies out there on a global level.
And yet we managed to get our foot in the door.
So what is it that you're providing to the service?
What is, what is it you're giving them?
Can you please repeat that?
You are.
So what, what is it that you're providing for these brands when you work with them?
What is the service that you're providing to them?
So what we're providing them is a clear description and understanding of reframing the question they have about recruitment according to the brain processes which lead to higher recruitment.
That's one thing.
And the second thing is we're providing them a solution which enables them to quantify their capacity to solve that challenge and the ingredients to then go and implement it.
The tools to go and achieve recruitment.
For example, maybe a good example is the project we did for PepsiCo has a British element to it.
So you know the lay's potato chips brand as the Most profitable snacking brand in the world.
And it's a tent pole for the whole PepsiCo organization.
The biggest media spend of the lace brand is the Champions League football contract.
They have.
They're one of the main sponsors of Champions League football.
Their biggest media contract lies there.

What they have been doing with that contract, how they fill it in, how they use it to convey information from the brand to the consumer via the Champions League platform is by large determined by the work we did for lace.
For instance, the TV spot that they broadcast is one of the most important vehicles then of, for information for that, for that brand.
We don't make the spot.
The spot is made by one of the big agencies in London.
It's bdbo, the next to the Tate Museum there, their offices.
Well, we were able to convince Lays of the value of what we do, of the added value.
And our work served as a very detailed briefing for the agency to develop the tvc, but much tighter than a usual agency briefing, much more precise.
The type of scenes, the type of interaction between, or social interaction between the people playing within the commercial, the roles of their brand ambassadors in the commercial.
So Messi and Pogba, all of this was determined by our work?
Yeah, the use of sound was an important component.
But all of that follows a completely different development part than the classical development part in the advertising world.

All of it comes out of a system, a scientific setup that allows to sort of quantify, identify and amplify the components of a message, in this case a commercial, to really touch consumers on a much deeper, much fundamental psychological level.
So the fact alone that we are trusted with this mission, such a high stakes game is already pretty exceptional.
Doesn't happen a lot that small entities like us are trusted with that work.
But even more amazing is that this work afterwards led to the most performant campaign of LACE ever.
And we have client testimonials on that.
This isn't, these aren't our words.
These are the words of the client.
And then that was done about four years ago and they're still using the basis of our work to reiterate these campaigns.
So that's just one example.
Now, of course, we can't go into the real detailed explanation of how we do it today because we don't have an NDA with you and it would take too long.
Does that help you understand?
A little bit.
You're on mute, I think, Andy.
Sorry about that.
Yeah.
DOG BARKED yeah, so it helps a little bit.
What is it you're, you're trying to do there you want to sell the IP to somebody else and what, do what with the money?
Are you looking to reinvest in the business?
Are you looking to, to leave?
No, we're very much wanting to stay.
If that would be a possible scenario, that would for us be very good.
But what we seek is we see ourselves as inventors and what we've done during 10 years is developing, inventing, crafting this IP to its current form.
So all the underlying science is nice, but it crystallizes down to.
Yeah, it's, it's really, it has the substance to take the whole industry from something that is not science based towards something that is science based.

So to go back to my example of the doctor who tries to treat your diabetes without the proper knowledge of the underlying metabolic processes, we can take this industry, or whoever acquires it, has the substance to take this industry from where it is today towards is a practice which is much more aligned, much more science based, much more data based than it is today.
And for that we seek a partner who has the capacity, but also the willingness to roll this out in an ambitious manner.
The type of partner we're looking at, our vision, but you might see it in a different way would be major research agencies, major consultancies, brand owners potentially and communication.
Yeah, communication.
Communication, ecosystems.
Okay, so sounds hugely interesting.
Obviously you've not really told me much, but told me a lot at the same time.
So.
The thing is, at the end of the day, we, you're looking for value for your ip, right?

So what you do is from a science background and from an inventor's process and arguably it's a different approach to where other agencies may just vibe and come up with a solution that works, but they don't know why, you know, more divining rods than science, but they, they're kind of getting to the same space.
Now.
The buyers of your IP will probably see the value in what you're, you know, what you're offering, but they're going to say, okay, how much is it worth and why is it worth that price?
Whereas an agency, traditional agency, which is, I don't know, I don't know how much revenue you're doing, but let's just say you're doing 5 million revenue.
There's an agency with doing 5 million revenue, they're 30 people and they come up with this solution and another business would buy them for, you know, five times multiple on their ebitda.

So the, the issue that we're going to hit is, you know, why do these guys think their IP is worth XYZ when the result is the same as an agency's approach, which is using the divining rods, but still gets there.
And we know that they're worth 5 million because that's how you value agencies performance.
Yeah, EBITDA.
So, so really what I need to know is how much is your revenue, how much is your, your profit margin?
I guess if you're, if you're massively apart from that, you know, with your own valuation on the ip, then I probably can't help you.
If it's within the part, then yeah, happy to just run a process where we find buyers.
That's exactly what we do.
Okay.
Before touching on the point of the business, just to build on your point of another agency, you could come to the same conclusion through luck.

The problem is, is imagine you were the only owner of the other agency or of our agency and you would step into the room for a briefing from a client such as a lays and you'd be able to explain to that client those brain processes.
For the first time ever.
They would hear this right?
They would understand that you have complete authority within this domain of how to develop content for a TV commercial which will have the highest impact possible on the brain processes.
Not only that, but then you have the toolkit to go and quantify which components, which elements, which type of information will achieve that goal.
The other agency comes in the room, they don't have that, they don't have that knowledge.
They might have a nice track record, but they don't have that knowledge.
You have the track record and you have all this authority.
Which agency would win the pitch most oftenly?
The one with the nicest creative probably.

So that, I mean that that might be the problem is that people that sat on the other side of the table, they don't care about the brain functions, they just want to get the result and they want to get there in an exciting novel way.
And they pick agencies that come up with novel solutions and nice pictures and things that make them feel excited too.
So arguably there is a lot of witches and wizards in the industry and you guys are the scientists and the doctors and there's two different approaches and for sure both of them work.
What we're definitely seeing within the industry is there's much more measurement and data that is into what the creatives are guided by.
And I guess you guys would be on that side of the fence and there were plenty of buyers for those types of things.
But again they boil down to multiples of actual businesses.

So I Think for my sake because I've only got so long and I just want to really understand it from my point of view because the answer with my me is probably fairly binary is I can help you or I can't.
Yeah, yeah, understand it.
I can't sell IP that has no financial value.
Okay.
And that, and that I understand it and I respect that.
This is your approach.
In our case the revenue is extremely low.
It's under a million what we do, but we don't have a business, it's a laboratory.
So three, four projects per year.
But we choose those projects very carefully in order to build proof of concept for the claims we make.
So for instance, value for money is crucial component of brand management.
Specifically for FMCG brands for instance, the best available tool on the market is ridiculously primitive compared to the tool that we have built.
It's not we who say it, it's high level executives at Unilever for instance who say that.
Can I just say right, there's two things.
Firstly the fact that you're a laboratory, that that's absolutely fine.
You know the majority of my clients that are forward thinking they have a labs part.
You know, they have a department that just focuses on R and D, new stuff.
So, so that isn't necessarily a foreign.
Okay.
But the other the, the argument is really if Unilever are so invested with your process, why have they not spent millions doing using it if it, if it works so well?
So what I can't do is take two guys into a room and say you've got to buy these guys IP because they work with all of these companies and they've all said that they, these guys are the bees knees.
But they haven't done anything financially yet because they're just collecting data and they're working at a really slow pace.
Everybody is going to say to me that's great.
They look, they look great.
They've generated I don't know what.
You still haven't given me a number.
It's between 500 and 800 per year.
Depends a bit where we dedicate.

They generate on average 600k a year and the profit margin is massive because it's just them two and their laboratory and so they'll be able to put a value on that and that's fine, but it wouldn't be.
What I can't do is walk in that room and say this is the IP and we're shooting for 10 million because it's worth 100.
They're just going to laugh Me out of the room.

So if you prepare to accept a process where they're going to give you a multiple based on your profit margin, which is going to be quite good for the size of the business, but it's going to be a low multiple because of this business.
Of course, we're not interested in that at all.
Yeah, I don't feel I can help you.
But just, just to build on what you're saying is that there are processes to value IP.
Yeah, there are.
Which are.
We don't sell IP to marketing agencies ever.
I've never sold IP to them.
We sold them SaaS businesses and they have better multiples.
And we sold the measurement businesses and they have better multiples.
But it's always based on something that they.
Financially, what it's not based on is, can this idea change the world?
Is it worth 20 billion?
Okay, we're going to give these guys 5 billion because we're going to exploit another 15 billion.
I can't get that deal done for you.
I'm not an IP expert.
The people that buy from us are marketing agencies and, and private equity.
But they, they buy based on those financial principles and I can't, I can't change that.
I understand that and, well, I can't sell them ideas.
Fair enough.
So let's give it some thought.
But based on the low revenue we have, boom.
The profit margins are high and because there are costs, but even a high multiple of that doesn't come near the ambition that we have.
So our members, then I think you need to still do some work to show what your ambition is.
And part of that is exploiting the idea that you, you have financially.
You know, I think the argument here is if you can take it into Unilever and they're telling you it's the best thing ever, then we'll, we'll go and license across.
Are you interested, Are you interested in hearing why Lace never bought another project from us?
Because that's what happened.
Yeah, go on.
They just used your ideas and discounted.
Well, they paid it and they, they know that they participate in sort of experiment for us, building proof of concept of the IP in this specific context.
It was proving its validity to create campaigns in a better manner than the traditional development manner.
So I explained you how high the stakes were of the project and so on.
So the guy delivers the best performing campaign ever.
His superiors congratulate them.
Yeah.
How is it done and who has worked on it and so on.
And he explains that he worked with this extremely innovative way of doing Things and worked with a company that nobody knows.
Well, the guy almost lost his job because of that.
His boss said, are you crazy to trust nobody's with such a high stakes thing?
And says, yeah, but based on my assessment of the situation, my colleague's assessment of the situation, this could only lead to great things, which it has, so let's, let's embrace it and exploit it.
No, we're not doing that.
We stick to how things have always been done here, which is a reality, and it will be an obstacle in the growth and rollout of this thing.
But it's the enemy here.
Or the answer to your question here, why hasn't it become such a massive thing despite it being so strong?
Is the inertia of the industry.
It's really the inertia of the industry.
It's much more conservative.
And it's also the grandeur, the elephant in the room that we're addressing.
Most people are not ready yet to be confronted with it.
When the messenger is nobody's like us.
And so the message is too big for the messenger.
That's, that's, that's our dilemma.
I think also you gave the analogy about the doctors not knowing how blood sugar works.
It's also like, I think the other, the other, the other side of that is like a marketing agency walking into a room full of surgeons that are about to perform an operation.

The patient is opened up and everybody's there saying, you know, what if you wore pink, if you had a nicer hat and maybe if we change the background and lit it a little bit nicer, that is the world that you're selling into.
So you've got a bunch of surgeons or doctors and scientists like yourself and the other side are holding their paintbrushes.
And you know, it's exactly that.
It is exactly that.

Look, I think it's fascinating, but I think at the end of the day, you have to either either accept that your, your valuation is based on the financials that you have at the moment, or if you can't accept that, you have to build the business yourselves to a point where it's worth something that you're willing to accept.
But at times, even with the people holding the paintbrushes, those people I speak to all think that their ideas are worth 10 times more than they are in real life.
So I'm saying that your ideas don't work and they're not worth that.
I'm sure they are, but there is just no way of me measuring that.
True.
Without you coming back and saying, well, these are our financials for the last 10 years and we've done tens of millions because everybody knows that it's true.
So it's just, yeah, I'm kind of just in a position where I don't believe that I can help you on this next bit just yet.
Understand that.
And unless you, unless you want to go through a sales process in which, in which case won't get the money that you want, but you'll certainly get inside a much larger business.
I'm sure that if we sold this into, you know, Iris Worldwide, for instance, they would love to, to have this as part of the labs department.
But you're not going to accept that you're not worth, I don't know, whatever your figure is.
10 million, 100 million.
They're not going to, they're not going to spend that.
They're just going to say, well these guys have generated 600,000.
That's kind of what they're worth.
One and a half times that maybe.
So, you know.
Yeah.
Do you have time for last counter argument?
You're eating up all my prep time for my next meeting.
Go on.
We are not remunerated in a way that a agency would be remunerated.
And we heard that time and time again that what we sell, we sell it at a fraction of cost that a bigger agency would be able to invoice for exactly the same service.
Another example, like the Volkswagen brand, still one of the top selling car brands in Europe.
We worked for them on a local level in Belgium, which we rarely do through personal contact for them.
We do a lot of work.

One of the latest things we did was a re slight repositioning of the brand, a very strategic exercise and it went in against the global directives the Belgium team gets from the German global headquarters.
So already our work is so convincing for the Belgium team that ready to push against the directives of Global HQ, which rarely happens.
Of course.
Global HQ sees what happens in Belgium and asks an explanation.
Belgium team gives them the explanation.
We get to explain our stuff to the Global hq.
Global HQ is so impressed that they adapt the positioning of the Volkswagen brand in all European countries based on our work now impressive performance.
The financials of that are the invoice of a small local project in Belgium.
I think we charged them 60k or something for that work on which we still have a huge margin.
But it's a fraction of the invoice that a real high level consultancy who is normally hired to do this type of work charges.
It's more than 10 that they would add to the invoice.
Which I totally get that.
But again that's not something I can help you directly with.
You are in a position that a lot of creatives are in.
For instance, there might be a branding or design agency who do all of the strategy work for major brand and they get paid millions.
Their budget will be, you know, there's 5 million budget go and rebrand something from Pepsi and they will use that money to go and find a lot of small agencies to do all of the work.
Because their, their strategy will be the overarching thing that goes the brand that's worth millions.
All of the, the dog's body work that's performed by the actual creatives that actually, actually do the work that they get paid next to nothing.
And it happens across all industries but particularly in.
So the thing for you guys is to reposition yourselves as a company that.
You paused again or I paused.
Chat or something.
Sorry.
I'm on Elon Musk's satellite dish.
I'm in the countryside.
It cuts out for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.
So you know, the onus is really on you guys to reposition the business as a strategic.
So that you, you're not taking the money at the bottom, you know, that you're taking the overarching, you know, and that's on you guys to reposition the business.
Okay.
You know, advice.
Well, I feel for you but you know, and I don't.
I think what you're feeling are like science issues and regional issues and small issues are actually just the same issues that all businesses have when they're starting up.
And it's not necessarily you're being singled out for being different, it's just that that's the way that business works.

And hopefully if you can reposition yourself as one of those strategic agencies and I don't know whether that's possible with what you do but it seems, I mean the front end of your website is very like a marketing agency's website.

So I think maybe you need to go in at a strategic level and charge strategic prices and, and just build a big bigger business or you end up doing consultancy work for project budgets that are 50, 000.
Okay, thank you, thank you for that advice.
We appreciate it.
Keep all our options open.
So always I don't know if it's of any value.
I guess you guys are very strong minded and you're just going to do it your own way which is absolutely fine.
So we wouldn't be inventors otherwise.
Who am I to interfere but if you ever think.
Do you know what?
Let's just go and get and sell our business.
For a reasonable amount of money, I will find a home in a big agency, and they would be happy to have you as their labs.
Okay.
Happy to hear that.
Yeah.
I appreciate it.

summary.action_items:
**Nathan Axford**
Consider Andy's advice about repositioning the business at a strategic level to command higher fees (35:26)
Evaluate whether to accept a valuation based on current financials or continue building the business (34:32)
Decide whether to explore selling the business to a larger agency that would value their 'labs' approach (35:42)

**Andy Day**
Remain available if Nathan decides to pursue a more traditional valuation and sale process (35:42)
summary.overview: In the Business Development / Exploratory Sales Discussion meeting between Nathan and Andy, Andy Day from Capital A, a UK-based M&A firm specializing in marketing agencies, provided an overview of his company's operations and focus on the U.S. market. Nathan presented his innovative approach that integrates neuroscience with marketing strategy to enhance consumer engagement, referencing successful projects with major brands, including PepsiCo. The conversation transitioned to valuation challenges, where Andy highlighted the discrepancy between Nathan's current revenue and his business's valuation expectations, stressing the importance of traditional financial metrics in M&A. He advised Nathan to consider repositioning his business for higher fees or accept a valuation that reflects current financials. The meeting concluded with Nathan acknowledging Andy's insights and remaining open to future opportunities, while Andy expressed readiness to assist should Nathan decide to pursue a sale. Action items for Nathan include evaluating his business's strategic positioning and potential sale to a larger agency, while Andy will be available to support if necessary.
